claims.claim: Sgo1 is needed to preserve Sgo2-PP2A-B56 at the centromere.
claims.source: Finally, Sgo1 is needed to preserve Sgo2-PP2A-B56 at the centromere (Figure 2e) and it can also bind directly to the SA2–Scc1 complex (Hara et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013b; Tanno et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is shown by data in Figure 2e.

claims.claim: Sgo1 can bind directly to the SA2-Scc1 complex.
claims.source: Finally, Sgo1 is needed to preserve Sgo2-PP2A-B56 at the centromere (Figure 2e) and it can also bind directly to the SA2–Scc1 complex (Hara et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013b; Tanno et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: This is cited from Hara et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013b; Tanno et al., 2010.

claims.claim: Sgo1 may help to position Sgo2-PP2A-B56 so that it can dephosphorylate nearby residues within the cohesin complex.
claims.source: Therefore, perhaps Sgo1 also helps to position Sgo2-PP2A-B56 so that it can dephosphorylate nearby residues within the cohesin complex.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the known interactions.

claims.claim: The LxxIxE binding pocket is completely conserved in all B56 isoforms.
claims.source: Although the LxxIxE binding pocket is completely conserved in all B56 isoforms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we observe a striking preference in the binding of B56γ over B56α to many LxxIxE containing proteins during prometaphase (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is shown by sequence alignment in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: There is a striking preference in the binding of B56γ over B56α to many LxxIxE containing proteins during prometaphase.
claims.source: Although the LxxIxE binding pocket is completely conserved in all B56 isoforms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we observe a striking preference in the binding of B56γ over B56α to many LxxIxE containing proteins during prometaphase (Figure 4).
claims.evidence: This is shown by immunoprecipitation data in Figure 4.

claims.claim: Binding between LxxIxE motifs and B56α is repressed during prometaphase.
claims.source: We hypothesise that this is due to repressed binding between LxxIxE motifs and B56α during prometaphase, because LxxIxE binding (Figure 6e,f) and kinetochore accumulation (Figure 5h,j) can both be enhanced by mutation of the EPVA loop in B56α (B56αTKHG).
claims.evidence: This is hypothesized based on the data in Figure 6e,f and Figure 5h,j.

claims.claim: Sgo2 interaction is unlikely to obscure the LxxIxE binding pocket in B56α.
claims.source: Considering that this region also controls Sgo2 and centromere binding, a simple explanation could be that Sgo2 interaction obscures the LxxIxE binding pocket. However, this appears unlikely for four reasons: 1) Sgo2 depletion does not relocalise B56α to kinetochores (Figure 2a,b), 2) Sgo2 depletion does not enhance the ability of B56α to bind to BubR1 or other LxxIxE motifs during mitosis (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), 3) centromere and kinetochore binding can occur together in certain B56α-γ chimaeras (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b), and 4) the regions that define each of these localisations do not fully overlap (Figure 6g).
claims.evidence: This is concluded from multiple lines of evidence in Figures 2, 6.

claims.claim: Another interacting partner or a tail region within a PP2A-B56 subunit might obscure or modify the conformation of the LxxIxE binding pocket in PP2A-B56α complexes.
claims.source: If not Sgo2, then what could limit the kinetochore accumulation of B56α? We speculate that another interacting partner, or alternatively a tail region within a PP2A-B56 subunit, might obscure or modify the conformation of the LxxIxE binding pocket in PP2A-B56α complexes.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism.

claims.claim: Sgo1 contributes to the B56γ signal observed at the kinetochore.
claims.source: An important additional finding of this work is that Sgo1 contributes to the B56γ signal observed at the kinetochore (Figure 3g–j).
claims.evidence: This is shown by experimental data in Figure 3g-j.

claims.claim: Sgo1's contribution to kinetochore B56γ likely requires Sgo1 to be bound to histone tails.
claims.source: This likely requires Sgo1 to be bound to histone tails, because it also depends on Bub1, the kinase that phosphorylates histone H2A to recruit Sgo1 (Baron et al., 2016; Kawashima et al., 2010; Kitajima et al., 2005; Liu et al., 2013a; Tang et al., 2004; Yamagishi et al., 2010) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and cited from prior work.

claims.claim: The interfaces between BubR1-B56 and Sgo1-PP2A-B56 do not appear to be overlapping based on current structural data.
claims.source: The interfaces between BubR1-B56 and Sgo1-PP2A-B56 do not appear to be overlapping, at least based on current structural data (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Xu et al., 2009), which implies that Knl1-bound BubR1-B56 could potentially be anchored towards histone tails by Sgo1.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from structural data cited from Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Xu et al., 2009.

claims.claim: Knl1-bound BubR1-B56 could potentially be anchored towards histone tails by Sgo1.
claims.source: The interfaces between BubR1-B56 and Sgo1-PP2A-B56 do not appear to be overlapping, at least based on current structural data (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Xu et al., 2009), which implies that Knl1-bound BubR1-B56 could potentially be anchored towards histone tails by Sgo1.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on structural considerations.

claims.claim: This is the first time that sub-functionalization has been demonstrated between isoforms of the same B family.
claims.source: This is the first time that such sub-functionalisation has been demonstrated between isoforms of the same B family.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claims.claim: The use of different B56 isoforms may allow PP2A catalytic activity to be regulated differently in specific subcellular compartments.
claims.source: One possibility is that the use of different B56 isoforms allows PP2A catalytic activity to be regulated differently in specific subcellular compartments: for example, by enabling interactions or post-translational modifications that are specific for the B56 subunits.
claims.evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of isoform-specific localization.

claims.claim: Protein inhibitors of PP2A-B56 have been shown to function specifically at the centromere (SET) and at the kinetochore (BOD1).
claims.source: In this respect, protein inhibitors of PP2A-B56 have been shown to function specifically at the centromere (SET (Chambon et al., 2013)) and at the kinetochore (BOD1 (Porter et al., 2013)); therefore, it would be interesting to test whether these inhibitors display selectivity for certain PP2A-B56 isoforms.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Chambon et al., 2013 and Porter et al., 2013.

claims.claim: The recent development of selective inhibitors of related PP1 regulatory isoforms to combat neurodegenerative diseases provides proof-of-concept that successful targeting of specific serine/threonine phosphatase isoforms is both achievable and therapeutically valuable.
claims.source: The recent development of selective inhibitors of related PP1 regulatory isoforms to combat neurodegenerative diseases (Das et al., 2015; Krzyzosiak et al., 2018), provides a proof-of-concept that successful targeting of specific serine/threonine phosphatase isoforms is both achievable and therapeutically valuable.
claims.evidence: This is cited from Das et al., 2015 and Krzyzosiak et al., 2018.

results.result: The manuscript establishes the background knowledge about PP2A-B56 structure and function during mitosis, including its role in regulating sister chromatid cohesion, kinetochore-microtubule attachment, and the spindle assembly checkpoint through interactions with BubR1 at kinetochores and Sgo1/Sgo2 at centromeres.
results.evaluation: These claims (C1-C3, C12-C15, C17-C28) represent well-established prior knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. The claims accurately describe PP2A structure, B56 regulatory subunit diversity, and the known roles of PP2A-B56 in mitotic processes. The citations appear appropriate and the background is consistent with current understanding of PP2A-B56 function.

results.result: Different B56 isoforms display differential subcellular localization during prometaphase, with B56γ and B56δ localizing predominantly to kinetochores (marked by Cenp-C), B56α and B56ε localizing mainly to centromeres (defined by Sgo2), and B56β showing mixed localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C7 are directly supported by immunofluorescence imaging and line plot quantification shown in Figure 1a,b. The data clearly demonstrate distinct localization patterns for different B56 isoforms using appropriate markers (Cenp-C for kinetochores, Sgo2 for centromeres). The quantitative line plots provide rigorous spatial analysis across the centromere-kinetochore axis.

results.result: Only centromere-localized B56α, but not kinetochore-localized B56γ, can support proper centromeric cohesion when other B56 isoforms are depleted.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C34 are supported by chromosome spread analysis in Figure 1c showing that cells retaining only B56α maintain centromeric cohesion while those retaining only B56γ show cohesion defects similar to complete B56 depletion. The functional specificity correlates with the differential localization patterns, providing strong evidence for isoform-specific roles.

results.result: Only kinetochore-localized B56γ, but not centromeric B56α, can support SAC silencing (Knl1-MELT dephosphorylation and mitotic exit) when other B56 isoforms are depleted.
results.evaluation: Claims C38-C42, C47 are supported by multiple complementary assays in Figure 1d-f: enhanced basal Knl1-MELT phosphorylation, delayed MELT dephosphorylation upon Mps1 inhibition, and prevented mitotic exit following B56 depletion are all rescued by preserving B56γ but not B56α. The data demonstrate clear functional specificity with appropriate controls and quantification.

results.result: B56γ, but not B56α, can rescue chromosome alignment defects caused by depletion of all B56 isoforms.
results.evaluation: Claims C44-C46 are supported by chromosome alignment analysis in Figure 1g showing that severe alignment defects following B56 depletion are rescued by preserving B56γ but not B56α. This provides additional functional evidence for isoform-specific roles at kinetochores, consistent with the SAC silencing data.

results.result: While endogenous B56α acts primarily at centromeres, overexpressed B56α can function at kinetochores due to elevated protein levels that overcome its normally restricted localization.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 reconcile apparent contradictions with prior literature (Foley et al., 2011) by demonstrating that overexpressed B56α shows elevated centromere and kinetochore levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 5) and can rescue kinetochore functions (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), while endogenous B56α cannot. This provides important context for interpreting overexpression studies and validates the isoform-specific model under physiological conditions.

results.result: Sgo2, rather than Sgo1, is the primary centromeric receptor for PP2A-B56 during mitosis, though Sgo1 contributes by helping to anchor the Sgo2-B56 complex at centromeres.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C61 are supported by systematic depletion experiments in Figure 2a-g showing that Sgo2 depletion significantly reduces centromeric B56α while Sgo1 depletion causes spreading toward kinetochores, and combined depletion completely removes B56α. The line plot analysis provides rigorous spatial quantification. This challenges the prevailing view that Sgo1 is the primary receptor and is appropriately supported by citation to Kitajima et al., 2006.

results.result: Sgo2 displays selectivity for B56α over B56γ, as demonstrated by CB-Sgo2 recruiting only B56α and B56α (but not B56γ) co-recruiting endogenous Sgo2 in targeting assays.
results.evaluation: Claims C62-C64 are supported by two complementary in-cell interaction assays (Figure 2h-m): CB-Sgo2 recruitment experiments and dCas9-DARPin co-recruitment assays. Both approaches demonstrate selective interaction between Sgo2 and B56α but not B56γ, providing mechanistic explanation for differential centromere localization. The use of orthogonal methods strengthens the conclusion.

results.result: BubR1 binding via the LxxIxE motif is necessary but not sufficient for B56γ kinetochore localization, as BubR1 depletion or H187A mutation reduces but does not eliminate B56γ at kinetochores, and Knl1/Bub1 depletion completely abolishes recruitment.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C70 are supported by systematic depletion and mutation experiments in Figure 3a-f and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c-f. The data show that disrupting BubR1 interaction leaves residual B56γ that spreads between kinetochore and centromere, while Knl1 or Bub1 depletion completely removes B56γ. This indicates additional anchoring mechanisms beyond the canonical BubR1-LxxIxE interaction.

results.result: Sgo1 collaborates with BubR1 to recruit B56γ to kinetochores through two separate arms: Bub1 binds BubR1 (which interacts with B56γ via LxxIxE) and Bub1 phosphorylates histone-H2A to recruit Sgo1 (which additionally anchors B56γ).
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C76, C116-C117 are supported by experiments showing Sgo1 depletion reduces B56γWT and eliminates B56γH187A at kinetochores (Figure 3g,h), the effect is specific to Sgo1 not Sgo2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1g,h), and B56γΔSgo1 mutation phenocopies Sgo1 depletion (Figure 3i,j). The model of dual recruitment arms through Bub1 is well-supported by the data and consistent with known Bub1 functions.

results.result: B56γ binds preferentially to BubR1 and other LxxIxE-containing proteins compared to B56α during prometaphase, likely due to repressed LxxIxE binding in B56α complexes rather than simple competition.
results.evaluation: Claims C77-C81 are supported by immunoprecipitation experiments (Figure 4a,b) showing reduced binding of multiple LxxIxE proteins to B56α compared to B56γ. The competition model is ruled out by showing B56α localization is unchanged when other isoforms are present or depleted (Figure 4c,d). The hypothesis of repressed binding in B56α is reasonable given the data, though the mechanism remains to be determined.

results.result: A small C-terminal loop containing four amino acids (EPVA in B56α vs TKHG in B56γ) at positions 405-425 is sufficient to switch B56 localization between centromeres and kinetochores.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C88 are supported by systematic chimera analysis (Figure 5) progressively narrowing the critical region to amino acids 405-425 and ultimately to a 4-amino acid loop. The B56αTKHG mutant switches localization from centromeres to kinetochores (Figure 5g-i) while maintaining function and holoenzyme assembly (Figure 5—figure supplement 2). This is a key mechanistic finding identifying the molecular determinant of differential localization.

results.result: The EPVA loop in B56α is necessary for Sgo2 interaction and centromere localization, and is also required to repress binding to LxxIxE motifs and kinetochore localization, as demonstrated by the B56αTKHG mutant losing Sgo2 binding while gaining LxxIxE binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 are supported by multiple assays showing B56αTKHG fails to be recruited by CB-Sgo2 (Figure 6a,b), cannot co-recruit endogenous Sgo2 (Figure 6c,d), but shows enhanced binding to LxxIxE proteins including BubR1 (Figure 6e,f). This demonstrates the EPVA loop has dual roles in promoting centromere binding and repressing kinetochore binding, providing mechanistic insight into isoform specificity.

results.result: The EPVA loop alone is not sufficient to switch localization; additional regions C-terminal (aa 414-453) and N-terminal (aa 374-386) to the EPVA are required for full centromere and kinetochore specification, respectively.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C97 are supported by additional chimera experiments (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) showing B56γEPVA does not switch localization, and defining the extended regions required for complete specification. This demonstrates the complexity of the localization determinants and shows the EPVA loop is necessary but not sufficient, requiring context from flanking sequences.

results.result: B56α binds preferentially to Sgo2 via a C-terminal region (aa 405-453) containing a critical EPVA loop that is unique to B56α and B56ε and conserved in Xenopus B56ε.
results.evaluation: Claims C101-C105 are supported by the chimera mapping data (Figure 5, Figure 6—figure supplement 1) identifying the critical region and EPVA sequence, sequence alignment showing EPVA is unique to B56α and B56ε (Figure 5g), and citation to Rivera et al., 2012 showing Xenopus B56ε selectively binds Sgo2. This provides evolutionary context and suggests conserved mechanisms of isoform-specific targeting.

results.result: Despite complete conservation of BubR1 and Sgo1 binding interfaces across all B56 isoforms, individual B56 isoforms localize differentially to kinetochores or centromeres, challenging the previous model of functional redundancy.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C32, C111 establish the paradox that motivated this study: conserved binding interfaces (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) yet differential localization (cited from prior work and demonstrated here). This apparent contradiction is resolved by the discovery of Sgo2 selectivity and the EPVA loop mechanism. The claims appropriately cite prior literature and set up the key question addressed by the manuscript.

results.result: Sgo1 can protect cohesion independently of PP2A by competing with WAPL, and may help position Sgo2-PP2A-B56 for dephosphorylation of cohesin complex residues through direct binding to SA2-Scc1.
results.evaluation: Claims C106, C109 are supported by citations to prior work (Hara et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2013b; Tanno et al., 2010). Claim C108 is supported by data in Figure 2e. However, claims C107 and C110 are speculative interpretations not directly tested. While the speculation is reasonable given the data, the proposed mechanisms for how Sgo1 helps cells tolerate Sgo2 loss and positions Sgo2-PP2A-B56 require additional experimental validation.

results.result: Binding between LxxIxE motifs and B56α is repressed during prometaphase, likely not by Sgo2 obscuring the binding pocket but possibly by another interacting partner or conformational changes within PP2A-B56α complexes.
results.evaluation: Claim C113 is a hypothesis supported by the B56αTKHG data (Figure 6e,f, Figure 5h,j). Claim C114 presents four lines of evidence arguing against Sgo2 obscuring the LxxIxE pocket, which are reasonable but not definitive (e.g., Sgo2 depletion experiments in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 may not fully rule out conformational effects). Claim C115 is pure speculation about alternative mechanisms. The model is plausible but requires further mechanistic investigation.

results.result: Based on structural data, the BubR1-B56 and Sgo1-PP2A-B56 binding interfaces do not overlap, suggesting Knl1-bound BubR1-B56 could potentially be anchored toward histone tails by Sgo1.
results.evaluation: Claim C118 is based on inference from published structural data (Wang et al., 2016a; Wang et al., 2016b; Xu et al., 2009) showing non-overlapping interfaces. Claim C119 is speculation about a potential ternary complex. While the structural inference is reasonable, the proposed model of Sgo1 anchoring BubR1-B56 to histone tails is not directly tested and remains hypothetical. The authors appropriately note they could not detect Sgo1 in BubR1 immunoprecipitates.

results.result: Background on SAC activation, PP2A-B56 antagonism of SAC signaling, kinetochore-microtubule attachment, and the roles of Sgo1/Sgo2 in cohesion protection.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C37, C43, C53-C54, C71 represent established background knowledge appropriately cited from the literature. These claims provide necessary context for understanding the experimental results but do not represent novel findings of this study. The citations appear accurate and the background is consistent with current understanding.

results.result: Discussion of the broader significance of B56 isoform sub-functionalization, including prior observations of differential localization, potential mechanisms for isoform-specific regulation, and therapeutic implications.
results.evaluation: Claims C98-C99 appropriately cite prior observations of differential B56 localization in other contexts. Claim C100 is reasonable speculation about evolutionary significance. Claim C120 asserts novelty of demonstrating sub-functionalization within the same B family. Claims C121-C123 discuss potential mechanisms and therapeutic implications with appropriate citations. These discussion points are well-supported and place the findings in broader context.

results.result: Summary of the main findings: centromeric B56 isoforms rely on Sgo2 interaction, kinetochore isoforms bind BubR1/LxxIxE motifs, Sgo1 helps anchor PP2A-B56 at both locations, and a small C-terminal loop regulates these interactions.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C11 represent summary statements of the main findings that are supported by the detailed experimental results described in other claim groups. These abstract-level claims accurately reflect the data presented in the manuscript and provide appropriate high-level conclusions from the work.
